extracted.intended_audience: researchers and meta-researchers studying peer review and scholarly publishing; journal editors; computational linguists and scientometricians performing large-scale text analyses of peer-review reports
extracted.subtask_short: linguistic analysis of peer review reports
extracted.subtask_description: Large-scale computational and statistical analysis of textual peer review reports (word count, linguistic tone, sentiment, and moral-language measures) to detect patterns associated with reviewer recommendation, field, review type, and reviewer gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of report (word count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Word count (mean and 95% CI) of peer review reports; used to compare reports by reviewer recommendation, area of research, peer review type and reviewer gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports recommending accept were shortest, major revisions longest. Include word count in models (used as random factor or covariate) and report summary statistics and CIs; check differences across fields and reviewer gender; see Supplementary file tables and Figure 1 for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical tone (LIWC)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC-derived standardized score (0–100) for 'analytical tone' indicating logical, hierarchical style of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High scores indicate analytical/scientific style (authors observed typical values ~85–91). Analytical tone varied with recommendation (higher for major revisions) and reviewer gender; report means, CIs, and mixed-model results; compare against baselines because scientific texts often show high analytical tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clout (LIWC)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC-derived standardized score (0–100) for 'clout', reflecting confidence, leadership or social status in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher clout = more confident tone; lower clout associated with tentativeness/insecurity. Reports recommending accept had highest clout; report field and gender differences and include mixed-model analyses (see Figure 2 and Supplementary files).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity (LIWC)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC-derived standardized score (0–100) for 'authenticity' where high authenticity reflects more personal, honest, humble writing (I-words, present tense, relativity words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low authenticity indicates more impersonal or potentially deceptive style. Social sciences reports showed higher authenticity; authenticity was also higher when reviewers recommended rejection. Provide examples of high/low-scoring texts (anonymized) and report statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional tone (LIWC) / LIWC sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC 'emotional tone' score (0–100) measuring prevalence of positive vs negative emotion words in the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher LIWC emotional tone indicates more positive affect; reports recommending accept had highest emotional tone. Present alongside other sentiment measures for validation; include means, CIs, and mixed-model tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: SentimentR sentiment score
rubrics_metrics.description: SentimentR package valence score (majority of scores range −1 to +1) indicating negative to positive sentiment in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as an independent sentiment measure; report distributions and compare against LIWC and CoreNLP outputs for convergence; include examples and statistical summaries (see Supplementary files 5–7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stanford CoreNLP sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stanford CoreNLP machine-learning sentiment score (0 negative to +4 positive) for emotional valence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a deep-learning-based sentiment measure for concurrent validity. Report concordance with LIWC and SentimentR and include examples illustrating score interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: General morality (LIWC + Moral Foundations)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC-derived measure for general moral-language prevalence (percentage of words related to morality) and log-scale summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports recommending accept had highest general morality scores. Because absolute prevalence is low (<1% for many moral categories), interpret cautiously and supplement with qualitative inspection; provide lists of most frequent moral words/phrases (Supplementary file 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five moral foundations (care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity)
rubrics_metrics.description: LIWC analysis using Moral Foundations Theory dictionaries to measure care/harm, fairness/cheating, loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, sanctity/degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors found minimal prevalence and no clear patterns across recommendations/fields. Note that many matches are common phrases not indicative of moral reasoning; recommend combining quantitative dictionary counts with qualitative or ML methods to assess moral content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation of sentiment methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple sentiment-analysis approaches (LIWC emotional tone, SentimentR, Stanford CoreNLP) and compare results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors used three approaches that produced similar results; use multiple methods to increase robustness and report convergent/divergent findings and examples illustrating each method's behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-model linear analysis with specified fixed and random factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed model linear analysis for each linguistic variable with fixed factors: reviewer recommendation, area of research, type of peer review, reviewer gender; random factors: journal, word count, article type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mixed models to control across-journal interactions, word count and article type; test interaction effects and present coefficients, residuals, and within-group standardized effect figures; be cautious interpreting small p-values given large N (consider effect sizes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset inclusion/exclusion and representativeness reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe source dataset (PEERE), number of reports, journal coverage, article types, filtering steps, and final sample composition (e.g., removal of reports with undetermined gender or missing recommendation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report counts at each filtering step (e.g., started with 583,365, excluded 110,636 for gender undetermined and 260 missing recommendation to reach 472,449). Describe field/journal biases (over-representation of health/medical and physical sciences, prevalence of single-blind review) and discuss implications for generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender determination / disambiguation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-stage gender inference: 1) use salutations when available; 2) query gender-guesser on first names and country; 3) query Gender API and accept returned gender when sample and accuracy thresholds met (minimum 62 samples and ≥57% accuracy) to keep misclassification <5%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report proportions from each source, rate of unknown gender, validation references, and expected misclassification. Use a validated workflow and document thresholds and rationale (see Santamaría & Mihaljević 2018).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymization, data sharing agreement, and privacy safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Data sharing governed by a PEERE protocol requiring agreements with publishers, data minimization, retention rules, privacy impact assessment, anonymization, restricted access, and aggregated reporting to avoid identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State data-access restrictions, provide contact for data controller, and document how anonymization and aggregation prevent identification of journals, publishers, or individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide anonymized example texts and LIWC score illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Show several LIWC scores paired with sample texts (preferably from dataset or, if privacy prevents, from publicly available referee reports) to demonstrate how LIWC categories map to actual text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these in an appendix or supplementary file; anonymize dataset examples when required; use external public reports (e.g., BMJ) if necessary to illustrate constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standardized LIWC constructs and document psychometrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the standardized version of LIWC with standardized scores and report psychometric properties (e.g., Cronbach's alphas) of LIWC constructs used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document which LIWC version was used, whether standardized constructs with acceptable reliability were used, and discuss LIWC limitations; where possible, validate LIWC measures using alternative methods (e.g., CoreNLP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish article/report types in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate original research peer reviews from other formats (opinion pieces, editorials, letters) and account for article type in analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use article type as a random factor or covariate (authors used it as a random factor); report N by article type and perform sensitivity analyses restricting to original research to check robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for subject-area and peer-review-type confounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Control for differences across research areas and review types (single-blind vs double-blind) because fields differ in report length and LIWC scores and review types are not evenly distributed across fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interaction terms and mixed models to disentangle effects; report that prior to controlling, physical sciences (predominant) may bias overall estimates; present within-field comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline comparisons and interpretive context
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide baseline corpora or reference points (e.g., typical scientific writing) to interpret descriptors such as 'cold and analytical'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare peer-review report scores to other scientific corpora or known LIWC benchmarks, and explicitly state what differences mean in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report limitations explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: State dataset and method limitations including field/journal sampling bias, predominance of single-blind review, lack of referee status/ expertise data, reliance on dictionary-based methods, and absence of manuscript content to assess review accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a limitations section, discuss how each limitation might bias findings, and suggest remedies (e.g., additional data or methods) for future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide full supplementary materials and transparency (tables, coefficients, examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply supplementary files with summary data, mixed-model coefficients, residuals, examples of high- and low-scoring reports, lists of most frequent moral words/phrases, and figures illustrating interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear links to supplementary files, label tables/figures, and ensure reproducibility by listing software versions and analytical code where possible (authors reported R v3.6.3 and package references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for multilevel/multidimensional analyses and reviewer profiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Go beyond group mean comparisons (bivariate ANOVAs) and use multilevel models, regression analyses, or reviewer-profile clustering to capture within-group variance and reviewer heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider building reviewer profiles (e.g., high clout + negative emotion + low analytical thinking) and assess where such profiles occur; present multilevel results to adjust for journals/fields and to detect multidimensional patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about statistical significance vs effect size in very large samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that very large N can yield statistically significant differences of trivial magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and interpret effect sizes and standardized differences, not only p-values; present figures of within-group standardized relations and discuss practical significance.
